questions.question: Q: What are the 4 Cs of food safety?

points.text: Cross-contamination prevention, Cleaning, Chilling, and Cooking.

questions.question: Q: What is the correct fridge temperature range?

points.text: 0–5°C, which keeps food below the danger zone to slow or stop bacterial growth.

questions.question: Q: Describe the correct handwashing procedure for food handlers.

points.text: Wet hands with warm water, apply soap, rub palms, backs of hands, between fingers, thumbs, and wrists for at least 20 seconds, rinse thoroughly, and dry with a clean paper towel.

questions.question: Q: Why should raw meat be stored on the bottom shelf of the fridge?

points.text: To prevent raw meat juices from dripping onto ready-to-eat foods below, which would cause cross-contamination.
Food should not be left in the danger zone (5–63°C) for more than a total of 90 minutes; it should be cooled rapidly and refrigerated.

questions.question: Q: Why should hot food not be placed directly in the fridge?

points.text: Hot food raises the fridge temperature, potentially bringing other stored foods into the danger zone and promoting bacterial growth.

questions.question: Q: What is stock rotation and which principle does it follow?

points.text: Stock rotation is organising food so the oldest products are used first. It follows the FIFO principle: First In, First Out.

questions.question: Q: What core temperature must food reach to be safe, and how should it be checked?

points.text: Food must reach a core temperature of at least 75°C (UK). It should be checked using a clean, calibrated food thermometer inserted into the thickest part of the food.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: The 4 Cs of food safety are Cross-contamination prevention, Cleaning, Chilling, and Cooking. Cross-contamination prevention involves keeping raw and ready-to-eat foods separate: using colour-coded chopping boards (e.g. red for raw meat), storing raw meat on the bottom fridge shelf so juices cannot drip onto other foods, and washing hands thoroughly after handling raw foods. This prevents harmful bacteria transferring from contaminated to safe food. Cleaning means washing and disinfecting all surfaces, utensils, and equipment before and after food preparation, as well as maintaining personal hygiene — washing hands with soap and warm water for at least 20 seconds, wearing clean aprons, and covering cuts with blue waterproof plasters. This removes bacteria from surfaces and hands, reducing the risk of transfer. Chilling means keeping perishable food below 5°C in the fridge (or −18°C in the freezer) to slow or stop bacterial multiplication, and following the 90-minute rule so food does not remain in the danger zone (5–63°C) for extended periods. Cooking means heating food to a core temperature of at least 75°C, checked with a food thermometer, to kill most harmful bacteria. Together, the 4 Cs address each stage where food safety can be compromised and form the foundation of safe food practice.
